overview: Tesco is the UK's largest grocery retailer, operating 3,724 stores across the UK, Republic of Ireland (ROI), and Central Europe (Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia), alongside the Booker wholesale business, dunnhumby data/insights, Tesco Mobile, Tesco Bank's successor Insurance and Money Services (IMS) arm, and the Clubcard loyalty programme. Revenue of roughly £73.7bn (FY2025/26, 53 weeks) is generated predominantly through UK & ROI retail (~80% of sales), with Booker wholesale (~14%) and Central Europe (~7%) providing diversification. Tesco exited consumer banking in November 2024, selling the retail banking business (credit cards, loans, savings) to Barclays while retaining insurance, travel money, ATMs and gift cards under the IMS banner.

business_model.summary: Tesco earns most of its profit from UK & ROI food and general merchandise retail (large stores, convenience, online grocery and rapid delivery via Whoosh), supplemented by Booker's wholesale/cash-and-carry distribution to caterers and independent retailers, Central European retail, and increasingly capital-light revenue streams: dunnhumby data analytics/retail media, Tesco Mobile (MVNO with O2), Tesco Media and Insight advertising, and Insurance and Money Services (travel money, ATMs, life/home/travel/pet/car insurance underwritten via partners). Core grocery revenue is largely transactional/recurring (weekly shop habit, high Clubcard penetration of 84% in the UK), while wholesale and advertising revenue is more B2B in nature.
business_model.customer_type: Primarily B2C grocery/retail (millions of weekly shoppers, 24m+ UK Clubcard households) with a meaningful B2B wholesale arm through Booker (caterers, independent retailers, symbol groups Budgens/Londis/Premier) and B2B advertising/data clients via dunnhumby and Tesco Media.
business_model.geographic_mix: UK ~75-78% of sales, Republic of Ireland ~5%, Central Europe (Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia) ~7%, Booker UK wholesale ~14% (UK-domiciled); overwhelmingly a UK/Ireland business with modest Central European diversification.

competitive_position.market_position: UK's #1 grocery retailer by sales value, with market share of 28.5% (12 weeks to 22 Feb 2026, Worldpanel), up from 28.3% a year earlier and the highest level in roughly a decade; has gained share for 28+ consecutive four-week periods. ROI market share 24.2%, the fourth consecutive year of growth. Discounters Aldi and Lidl continue to hold roughly 18-19% combined share, remaining the main structural competitive threat to the traditional 'Big Four'.

moat_factors.description: Largest UK grocer with ~3,700 stores, the deepest supply chain and logistics network (incl. new Aylesford and planned London Gateway distribution centres), giving cost and range advantages competitors struggle to match at scale.

84% UK Clubcard penetration (87% ROI/Central Europe) generates granular purchase data monetized via dunnhumby and the fast-growing Tesco Media and Insight retail media platform; personalized 'Clubcard Prices' pricing increases switching costs and perceived value (customers save c.£404/year on average).

Leading online grocery share (36.9% UK, +112bps YoY) and rapid-delivery Whoosh service now covering ~73% of UK households, plus Booker wholesale reach into convenience/catering, gives Tesco optionality discounters lack.
107-year UK heritage, 'Every Little Helps' brand equity, consistently ahead of competitors on customer satisfaction/NPS tracking (YouGov, BASIS).

~60% of store selling space owned outright (estimated market value £17.7bn), providing balance-sheet flexibility (e.g., recent store buybacks) and a hedge against rising occupancy costs versus leasehold-heavy rivals.

weaknesses: Thin structural grocery margins (~4.3% Group adjusted operating margin) leave limited room to absorb cost shocks without price action or cost-cutting
Heavy UK concentration means Tesco is directly exposed to UK-specific regulatory, labour and consumer-spending risk with limited geographic offset
Discounters (Aldi/Lidl) continue to out-grow the overall market and compete structurally on cost, pressuring Tesco to match price investment (Aldi Price Match on 600+ lines) at a margin cost
High fixed-cost/lease-liability base (lease liabilities ~£7.9bn) increases sensitivity to inflation and interest rates

growth_drivers: Continued UK and ROI market share gains via sustained investment in price (Aldi Price Match, Clubcard Prices, Everyday Low Prices), quality (Finest range, double-digit growth for three years) and service
Online and rapid delivery expansion: UK online sales +11.2-11.4% YoY, Whoosh rapid delivery up 51-59% YoY and now covering ~73% of UK households, recently launched in Ireland

Capital-light, higher-margin digital/data revenue: Tesco Media and Insight retail media platform, dunnhumby, and AI-personalized Clubcard offers (13m+ customers receiving tailored offers, partnership with Adobe)
New digital adjacencies: Tesco Marketplace (migrated to Mirakl platform, basket spend +c.90%) and F&F Online, expanding addressable non-food/apparel revenue with limited capital intensity
Booker wholesale growth in core retail/catering and symbol brands (369 net new retailer partners in FY25/26), plus bolt-on M&A (Venus Wine and Spirit Merchants, acquired June 2024)
Supply chain modernization: new semi-automated Aylesford distribution centre and a new facility at DP World London Gateway (due 2029) to improve cost efficiency and availability
'Save to Invest' cost programme (c.£500-535m annual savings) funding reinvestment in customer offer while protecting margins
Capital returns: ongoing multi-year share buyback programme (£3.7bn cumulative since October 2021) supporting EPS growth alongside progressive dividend

business.risk: Discount competition from Aldi and Lidl
business.description: Structurally lower-cost discounters continue to take share from the broader market; Tesco must keep matching price investment (600+ Aldi Price Match lines), which is a direct, ongoing margin drag.

business.risk: Intense overall UK grocery competitive intensity
business.description: Seven UK retailers each hold over 5% market share; management explicitly flagged 'increased competitive intensity' in the UK market at the start of FY25/26, requiring incremental investment in value/quality/service.

business.risk: Customer, competition and markets principal risk
business.description: Company-identified principal risk: failure to understand changing customer behaviour or respond to the evolving competitive digital landscape could erode market share and brand trust.

Large holdings of customer/colleague data (Clubcard, IMS) create exposure to breach, fraud, and regulatory penalty; flagged as a top principal risk with increasing sophistication of threat actors (including AI-enabled attacks).

business.risk: Security of supply / supply chain disruption
business.description: Geopolitical tension, extreme weather, and supplier concentration could disrupt product availability; company has flagged an increased likelihood of 'minor disruption' events.

financial.description: Net debt rose to £(10,563)m at Feb-2026 (from £(9,454)m), pushing Net debt/EBITDA to 2.1x from 2.0x, partly due to returning ~£700m of Tesco Bank sale proceeds to shareholders via buybacks; lease liabilities (£7,884m) are the majority of net debt.

Principal UK pension scheme closed to accrual since 2015 moved from a net deficit of £(180)m to a net surplus of £220m in FY25/26, reducing but not eliminating long-term funding risk; triennial valuation showed 106% funding level, so no further deficit contributions required currently, but asset/discount-rate volatility could reverse this.

Group relies on ability to refinance debt and renew committed facilities (£2.5bn undrawn RCF to Nov 2027); rising rates increase net finance costs, which are expected to normalise upward now that Tesco Bank sale cash proceeds have been returned to shareholders.
Mark-to-market movements on inflation-linked lease derivatives created a £(26)m charge in FY25/26 versus £76m income the prior year, adding statutory earnings volatility.

regulatory.description: April 2026 business rates changes introduce a higher multiplier for large retail properties (rateable value >£500,000); most Tesco, Asda and Sainsbury's stores fall into this band, with industry estimates of a £350-600m annual cost increase across major grocers.

regulatory.risk: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) packaging levy and other new regulatory costs
regulatory.description: New EPR levy and increased employer National Insurance contributions were explicitly cited by management as incremental FY25/26 and FY26/27 cost headwinds, partially offset by the Save to Invest programme.

Principal risk includes compliance with grocery supply code, competition law and anti-bribery rules; an ongoing equal pay claim and other class-action-style litigation present financial and reputational risk.
EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR), UK Healthy Food Standard mandatory reporting proposals, and net-zero commitments could raise compliance costs over time.

macro.risk: UK consumer spending and cost-of-living pressure
macro.description: Subdued consumer confidence and continued cost-of-living pressure on UK/Irish households directly affects grocery volumes and basket mix; management explicitly cited 'continuing cost of living pressures' as a FY25/26 theme.

Tesco widened its FY26/27 adjusted operating profit guidance range (£3.0-3.3bn) explicitly citing uncertainty from the Middle East conflict and its potential impact on energy/food costs and household budgets.
Food commodity costs, energy and transport costs remain exposed to macro and weather-related volatility; principal risk explicitly named 'Macroeconomic exposures'.

Czech koruna, Hungarian forint and euro (ROI) exposure creates translation risk; FY25/26 Central Europe profit grew 2.7% at actual rates but fell (0.9)% at constant rates, showing FX can meaningfully swing segment results.

macro_factors.industry_outlook: UK grocery retail is a large, mature, low-growth, low-margin but resilient defensive industry (~4-5% sales growth nominal, driven mostly by food inflation and discounter-led volume share shifts) with structurally increasing bifurcation between full-range/convenience/online leaders (Tesco, Sainsbury's) and hard discounters (Aldi, Lidl) continuing to gain long-run share.
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate - grocery is a defensive, non-discretionary category, but general merchandise/clothing (F&F) and discretionary 'treat' spend (Finest, dining-in) show more sensitivity to disposable income and consumer confidence.
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - large lease liability base (~£7.9bn) and net debt (~£10.6bn) make financing costs sensitive to UK rates; higher rates also dampen consumer discretionary spend indirectly.
key_input_costs: Labour (UK National Living Wage increases, National Insurance contributions)

recent_developments.event: FY2025/26 full-year results: Group sales £66.6bn (+4.6% actual, +4.3% constant), adjusted operating profit £3,152m (+0.8%/+0.6% constant), adjusted diluted EPS 29.0p (+6.0%), free cash flow £1,957m (+11.8%), UK market share 28.5% (highest in roughly a decade), dividend per share 14.5p (+5.8%).

Guided FY2026/27 adjusted operating profit to £3.0-3.3bn, a wider-than-usual range explicitly reflecting uncertainty from the Middle East conflict; targeting c.£500m of further Save to Invest cost savings and medium-term free cash flow of £1.5-2.0bn.

H1 FY2025/26 interim results: Group sales £33,051m (+5.1%), adjusted operating profit £1,674m (+1.6% constant), adjusted diluted EPS 15.43p (+6.8%); raised FY25/26 adjusted operating profit guidance to £2.9-3.1bn from £2.7-3.0bn, citing better-than-expected customer response to price/quality investment and favourable weather.
UK market share rose to 28.4%, up 77bps YoY, marking 28 consecutive four-week periods of share gains; online market share rose to 36.9% and Whoosh rapid delivery sales grew 59% YoY.

UK business rates reform took effect from April 2026, introducing a higher multiplier for large retail properties; major grocers (Tesco, Asda, Sainsbury's) face an estimated £350-600m combined annual cost increase, with Tesco CEO Ken Murphy publicly lobbying for a broader rates overhaul.
Booker segment reporting change: following Group Executive Committee changes, Booker is now reported as a standalone operating segment (previously folded into UK & ROI) from H1 FY25/26 onward.

Completed the sale of Tesco Bank's retail banking operations (credit cards, loans, savings, ~£8.3bn unsecured lending, ~£6.7bn deposits) to Barclays Bank UK for consideration of ~£600m plus distributions, generating ~£1bn total cash proceeds; entered a 10-year exclusive partnership with Barclays to market branded credit cards, loans and savings products under the Tesco brand. Tesco retained Insurance and Money Services (travel money, ATMs, insurance). Returned ~£700m of proceeds to shareholders via additional share buybacks.
Booker acquired Venus Wine and Spirit Merchants, a specialist wine and spirits wholesaler, supporting catering channel growth.

guidance.as_of: FY2025/26 Full-Year Results (15 April 2026) and H1 FY2025/26 Interim Results (2 October 2025)

items.notes: Range deliberately widened versus normal practice to reflect uncertainty from the Middle East conflict and potential impact on energy/food costs and consumer spending; consensus prior to the update sat around £3.25bn, toward the upper end of the range. Builds on FY25/26 actual of £3,152m (52-week basis).
FY25/26 actual free cash flow was £1,957m (52-week basis), near the top of the prior range, prompting the upward revision.

items.vs_prior: continuation of ongoing programme (FY25/26 delivered c.£535m)
items.notes: Programme is the primary self-funding mechanism offsetting cost inflation (National Insurance, EPR levy, business rates, wage inflation) while continuing to invest in price/quality/service.
Continued investment in store estate refreshes, technology/digital capability, and distribution network (Aylesford, London Gateway).
Remains above UK statutory rate of 25% primarily due to non-qualifying depreciation.
FY25/26 benefited from one-off interest income on Tesco Bank sale proceeds before their return to shareholders via buybacks; that tailwind will not repeat.

items.target: Progressive dividend, targeting c.50% payout of adjusted EPS
items.notes: FY25/26 full-year dividend of 14.5p (+5.8%) consistent with policy.

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Ken Murphy emphasized confidence in the 'evolved strategy' (five strategic ambitions: winning in food; meeting more everyday customer needs; being the most strategic partner for suppliers; connected/personalised/loved by customers; long-term business sustainability), citing record UK market share and resilient customer satisfaction despite 'elevated' competitive intensity and cost-of-living pressure. CFO Imran Nawaz highlighted that the wider FY26/27 profit guidance range reflects genuine macro/geopolitical uncertainty (Middle East conflict) rather than a change in underlying trading momentum, and that normalization of net finance costs (loss of Tesco Bank sale interest income tailwind) is a headwind to watch.

bull_case: Tesco is gaining UK and Irish market share for the better part of three years running (highest UK share in roughly a decade at 28.5%), evidencing a durable, self-funded 'flywheel' of price/quality/service investment paid for by Save to Invest cost cuts

Scale and Clubcard data create a widening moat versus mid-tier competitors (Sainsbury's, Morrisons, Asda) and an emerging high-margin, capital-light growth engine in retail media/advertising (Tesco Media and Insight, dunnhumby) that is largely uncaptured in headline grocery margins

Strong and growing free cash flow (raised medium-term guidance to £1.5-2.0bn) funds a large, ongoing capital return programme (£3.7bn in buybacks since 2021) plus a progressive ~50%-payout dividend, supporting EPS growth independent of top-line

Exit from capital-intensive, lower-return consumer banking (Tesco Bank sale to Barclays) simplifies the balance sheet and risk profile while Tesco retains fee-like insurance/money-services income with less capital at risk
Owned property (c.60% of selling space, £17.7bn market value, a £0.7bn surplus to book value) provides balance-sheet optionality and downside protection versus leasehold-heavy peers
bear_case: UK grocery is a brutally competitive, structurally low-margin business (~4.3% adjusted operating margin); Aldi and Lidl continue to grow and any slip in Tesco's price investment risks renewed share loss

FY2026/27 guidance was explicitly widened (not just maintained) due to geopolitical uncertainty (Middle East conflict) and its potential impact on energy/food costs, signalling genuine downside risk to the margin outlook this year

New and rising UK-specific cost headwinds — business rates reform (est. £350-600m sector-wide), the Extended Producer Responsibility packaging levy, and higher employer National Insurance contributions — are a growing tax on retail profitability largely outside Tesco's control

Net debt/EBITDA ticked up to 2.1x as one-off Tesco Bank sale proceeds were returned to shareholders rather than retained, and net finance costs are expected to normalise upward now that the related interest-income tailwind has faded

Heavy reliance on the UK consumer means Tesco has limited geographic diversification to offset a UK-specific downturn in consumer confidence or a resurgence of food/energy inflation, and Central Europe has shown it can swing materially on FX and local competitive/regulatory pressure (constant-rate profit down (0.9)% in FY25/26)
